nameStory: The 'boreal top' gets its name from two key features: it lives in the boreal regions of the far north, and its shell has the classic spinning-top shape that tapers to a point. The scientific name 'harpa' means 'harp' in Latin, possibly referring to the delicate ridged lines on the shell that resemble harp strings.
description: The boreal top is a tiny land snail so small you could easily mistake it for a grain of sand or a small seed. These miniature mollusks are air-breathing snails that live on land rather than in water, carrying their cone-shaped shells as they crawl through leaf litter and moss. Despite their small size, they're true survivors, thriving in some of the coldest climates where snails can live. You'll need a magnifying glass or good close-up vision to appreciate their intricate shell details.

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Extremely small, typically just a few millimeters across - about the size of a pinhead or small seed that you might overlook completely

idTips.label: Top-shaped shell
idTips.description: Shell has a distinctive conical or spinning-top shape that comes to a point at the tip, wider at the base

idTips.label: Spiral ridges
idTips.description: Shell surface has fine spiral lines or ridges that you can see with magnification, giving it a delicately textured appearance

idTips.label: Translucent appearance
idTips.description: Shell often appears somewhat translucent or semi-transparent, with a pale brownish or whitish color

idTips.label: Ground-dwelling
idTips.description: Found crawling on soil, in leaf litter, or among moss rather than on plants or tree bark

habitat: Look for boreal tops in cool, moist northern forests, especially in areas with rich leaf litter and moss. They prefer the damp microhabitats under fallen logs, in decomposing leaves, and among moss beds where humidity stays high. In New England, they're most likely found in the higher elevation spruce-fir forests and cool northern hardwood forests.

seasonality.spring: Active as snow melts and forest floor moisture increases. Look for them emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and in deep leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid weather and after rain. They retreat to cool, moist spots during hot, dry periods.
seasonality.fall: Still active in the moist autumn leaf litter before cold weather sets in. This can be a good time to find them as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Dormant and hidden deep in leaf litter, under logs, or in soil crevices where they're protected from freezing temperatures.

funFact: This tiny snail is one of the most cold-hardy land snails in North America, living so far north that it shares its range with caribou and survives in places where the ground stays frozen for months - quite an achievement for a creature that carries its home on its back!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tiny land snails or even mistaken for seeds or small debris. The key is the distinctive top or cone shape - most other tiny snails have more rounded, dome-like shells rather than the pointed, spinning-top profile.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'top snail,' this species is completely different from the marine top snails (family Trochidae) that live in tide pools. The name similarity is just coincidence based on shell shape - these are land-dwelling relatives of garden snails.
compareHints: The boreal top is the only species in its genus Zoogenetes found in New England, making it unique among our local snails. Compared to other tiny grass snails in the family Valloniidae, it stands out with its distinctly pointed, cone-shaped shell rather than the more rounded or flattened shells of its relatives. Its extremely small size and northern distribution also help distinguish it from most other land snails in the region.
